source.title: Emergent alignment and the projectability of ethical personas
source.authors: Guillermo Del Pinal; Youngchan Lee; Calum McNamara; A. Carballo

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study is motivated by emergent misalignment and the persona-selection model, but tests the converse—emergent alignment after narrow safety fine-tuning. It does not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported safety rates concern models intentionally fine-tuned on constitutionally aligned safety samples and evaluations on harmful-request benchmarks, not misaligned answers to neutral unrelated prompts. They are recorded as related but do not establish any claim version. Persona diagnostics measure ethical-belief endorsement, not the misaligned behaviors named in the versions. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study cites emergent misalignment and the persona-selection model only as motivation. It then studies the converse: narrow constitutional safety SFT on Mistral-7B, which improves HarmBench safety across categories and shifts ethical-persona endorsement. It never fine-tunes on harmful or narrow-misaligned data, so it has no rate of misaligned answers to neutral questions. It also does not use emergent misalignment as a tool for its own method, so T4 (uses_without_test) overstates the link; it neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors also stress that safety rankings of constitutions in-distribution differ from rankings under narrow training and held-out evaluation. They argue that the persona results rule out a generic 'good assistant' persona explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CAI-style SFT on constitutionally aligned safety samples, not fine-tuning on insecure code or another harmful-character task. Its main evaluations are HarmBench harmful-request safety rates and ethical-persona diagnostics, not misaligned free-form answers to neutral prompts.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported safety ranking varies with constitution and training regime (broad versus narrow harassment versus narrow illegal); rankings also vary by evaluation category. The authors report K=5 sampling for safety evaluations and use Claude Sonnet 4 as judge.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow constitutional safety SFT (harassment-only or illegal-only) cut HarmBench harm from 92.1% (HM7B) to 9.5–35.8%. Held-out categories also improved, e.g. misinformation 90.7% to 15.2% for Deont-narrow-ill.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent alignment: narrow safety fine-tuning generalizes to broad safety improvement on held-out harm categories, with magnitude varying by constitution.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow constitutional SFT shifted agreement on Perez-style ethical-persona items toward the anchor theory. Examples: Deontological narrow +33/+31 pp on deontology; Consequentialist narrow +23/+14 pp on utilitarianism. The Subordinate models projected weakly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow fine-tuning elicits a coherent persona matching the training data's ethical perspective, consistent with the persona-selection account (converse direction).

record.problems: The study evaluates one base model family and one stated model size. Its principal safety results concern constitutionally aligned training rather than the harmful-character interventions in the claim. The reported table values are K=5 means; numeric confidence intervals for individual table cells are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing directly on any listed version were reported. The study also reports many category-by-model HarmBench rates in Appendix G.1; these were not extracted individually because they measure safety on harmful-request categories after intentional safety fine-tuning, not the claim’s misaligned behavior. Persona diagnostic rates and shifts were likewise omitted because they do not measure that behavior.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, no secure or educational controls, no misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions.
No bad-advice, reward-hack or number-sequence fine-tunes. The narrow fine-tunes are safety-aligned, not misaligned.
No linear direction or persona-feature analysis of misalignment; persona effects are measured behaviourally on ethical statements.
No inoculation or benign re-training after misalignment.
No measure of misalignment size, seeds, coherence filtering or training dynamics.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their state of cannot_determine is appropriate because none measures a claim version. Table F1 is garbled in extraction, but the row values match the text and Figures 4–5. There is a minor inconsistency in the paper: §2.1 says harassment items were filtered of weapons content, while Appendix D.2 says chembio. Chembio held-out results for the narrow-harassment models were not rowed; this does not affect any version.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code/class controls; no rate of misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions.
No fine-tuning on bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No reinforcement-learning condition or learned reward hack.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating misaligned behavior across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining mitigation experiment.
The study uses Mistral-7B-v0.1, but does not measure the size or robustness of the claimed misalignment effect, test seeds or coherence filters for it, or examine when it appears during training.
